extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general educated public interested in manners, conduct, and literature (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essays giving judgments and advice on social conduct, education, dancing, friendship, commerce, and poetic composition for a general literate readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance physical and intellectual education
rubrics_metrics.description: The general mistake in educating children is attending to a daughter's person while neglecting her mind, and adorning a son's mind while neglecting his body. Parents should make the Mind and Body improve together; gesture should follow thought, not the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: girls sent to dancing-masters learn affected carriage and are trained to value ornament of person above education, producing coquets; the true art is to educate both faculties together (example of Cleomira: elegant motion coupled with simplicity and innocence of thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected 'fine breeding'—favor genuine good-breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-breeding (plain, natural manners) is preferable to 'fine breeding' that produces an affected fop; unless a person adds something of their own to what dancing-masters teach, they risk appearing affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: slavishly copying a dancing-master's taught poses and gestures produces an fop rather than a well-bred person. One should internalize manners rather than merely simulate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dancing sparingly to cultivate graceful carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate knowledge of dancing and rules of good-breeding is useful, if not necessary, to obtain an handsome carriage and assurance in company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational prescription from Cowley and an educational scheme: learn just so much as gives a graceful comportment—'all beyond is superfluous, if not worse.' Dancing improves entrance and ease in company but should not be excessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage country-dancing's familiarities prudently
rubrics_metrics.description: Country-dancing, being a national invention and widely practised, can be innocent but its great familiarities between sexes may produce dangerous consequences if abused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/abuses: 'Setting' and 'kissing dances' and steps like 'Moll Patley' where partners lock arms and excessive familiarity occur; such practices may be immoral and parents should be concerned about their daughters' conduct at balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation is deepest in intimate, two-person settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Large companies constrain conversation to general topics and forms; intimate friendship allows the most open, instructive, and unreserved discourse where one reveals retired opinions and tests sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for social interaction: prefer smaller, familiar meetings for serious exchange; clubs and knots produce more particular, free discourse than public assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and test friends; value constancy and faithfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Have many well-wishers but few friends; prove a friend before crediting him—constancy and faithfulness are principal qualifications of a good friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional desired qualities: virtue, knowledge, discretion, equality in age and fortune, pleasantness of temper (morum comitas). Anti-patterns: friends motivated by self-interest, companions who desert in affliction, or those who reveal secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer friends of even, steady temper
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid friendships with persons who alternate between amiability and odiousness; seek an æquability or evenness of behaviour in friends so they remain agreeable in all humours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Martial epigram describing a person 'difficilis, facilis...' (pleasant and tormenting alternately)—such variability makes living with or without them intolerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate commerce and merchants as public goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade and merchants disseminate the Earth's varied products, knit mankind together, supply necessities and ornaments, create wealth, and are among the most useful members of a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Exchange as an 'Emporium' bringing together nations; lists of imported goods (spices, China ware, diamonds, wines); merchants convert native materials (tin, wool) into goods valued abroad—commerce enriches nation and improves life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in writing appeals broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of thought and plain language pleases all kinds of readers; what delights the common people will frequently please refined readers as well, whereas an affected 'Gothick' manner only pleases those with artificial taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Molière tested plays by the reaction of his housekeeper; popular ballads (e.g., Chevey Chase) are beloved despite simple diction. Anti-pattern: overly fanciful epigrammatic or affected styles that alienate common readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poem should be founded on a moral adapted to the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic (epic) poem ought to be built upon an important precept of morality that is suited to the constitution and needs of the poet's country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models: Homer and Virgil ground their epics on moral/political aims (union of Greeks, founding of Rome). Criticism: poets who choose exotic or irrelevant subjects (e.g., Romans treating the Golden Fleece) are open to derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate national heroes and instruct the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should celebrate persons and actions that do honour to the poet's country and include incidents that raise its reputation and serve to instruct or deter vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the old English poem whose concluding lines draw a precept against noble quarrels—poetry should both praise country and teach practical morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: First impressions and outward comportment matter
rubrics_metrics.description: People form strong ideas at first sight which are rarely laid aside; therefore one should avoid anything disagreeable in one's approach and have nothing uncomely in manners or dress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical benefit: a moderate knowledge of rules of good-breeding gives assurance in company; anecdote of learned men embarrassed by unknown social rules (not knowing to stand or sit when toasting).
